questiontext.text: What is the intent of the Singleton pattern?

answer.text: Ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global point of access to it

feedback.text: Correct — that is Singleton's defining intent.

answer.text: Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation

feedback.text: That describes Builder, not Singleton.

answer.text: Convert one class's interface into another interface a client expects

feedback.text: That describes Adapter, not Singleton.

answer.text: Attach additional responsibilities to an object dynamically

feedback.text: That describes Decorator, not Singleton.

generalfeedback.text: Singleton ensures a class has exactly one instance and provides a single global access point to it.

questiontext.text: Which mechanism is typically used to implement a Singleton?

answer.text: A private constructor plus a static getInstance() accessor

feedback.text: Correct — the private constructor blocks external creation and getInstance() returns the sole instance.

answer.text: A Director that sequences building steps

feedback.text: No — that belongs to the Builder pattern.

answer.text: A common component interface shared by leaf and composite nodes

feedback.text: No — that belongs to the Composite pattern.

generalfeedback.text: A private constructor prevents callers from using new, and a static getInstance() returns (and lazily creates) the single instance.

questiontext.text: What is a common concern when implementing a Singleton in a multithreaded program?

answer.text: Thread-safety of the lazy initialization

feedback.text: Correct — concurrent first calls could otherwise create more than one instance.

answer.text: Choosing the true median as a pivot

feedback.text: No — that is unrelated to Singleton.

answer.text: Keeping leaf and composite nodes uniform

feedback.text: No — that is a Composite concern.

generalfeedback.text: If two threads call getInstance() simultaneously during lazy init, they might each create an instance, so synchronization is needed.

questiontext.text: How does lazy initialization of a Singleton differ from eager initialization?

answer.text: Lazy creates the instance on first use; eager creates it at load/startup time

feedback.text: Correct — that is the lazy vs eager distinction.

answer.text: Lazy creates many instances; eager creates exactly one

feedback.text: No — both create exactly one instance.

answer.text: Lazy uses a Director; eager uses an Adapter

feedback.text: No — neither pattern is involved.

generalfeedback.text: Lazy initialization defers creation until the instance is first requested; eager initialization builds it up front.

questiontext.text: Which statements about Singleton are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: A private constructor prevents external code from creating new instances

feedback.text: Yes — that is how uniqueness is enforced.

answer.text: It provides a single global point of access to its one instance

feedback.text: Yes — that is part of Singleton's intent.

answer.text: It is intended to create many independent instances on demand

feedback.text: No — Singleton allows exactly one instance.

answer.text: It requires a Director to sequence construction steps

feedback.text: No — that is Builder, not Singleton.

generalfeedback.text: Singleton uses a private constructor and a static accessor to guarantee one instance reachable through a global access point.

questiontext.text: Singleton provides a global point of access to its single instance.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — a global access point is part of Singleton's intent.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Singleton explicitly provides a single global access point.

questiontext.text: A Singleton typically exposes a public constructor that any client may call with new.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — the constructor is made private so clients cannot create extra instances.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the constructor is private; access goes through the static accessor.

questiontext.text: The creational pattern that ensures a class has exactly one instance with a global access point is the ______ pattern.

answer.text: singleton

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: instance

feedback.text: Accepted — the single instance idea is the heart of the pattern.

answer.text: singleton*

feedback.text: Correct.
